This brought back memories for me. I remember as a teenager making many trips to West Berlin on the duty train. As we toured around the city it was amazing how the east attempted to escape to the west.
The saddest visit was one Easter I was looking into the east there was guards with guns watching the only person on the street which was a little girl riding a tricycle around the street below them. There were no cars or anyone with the little girl.
There was a group of West Germans on the tower with us speaking German. I really felt they might have been family. It was during the time that the border was closed  between the east and west. In 75 I was back in Germany with my husband. The border was opened and it was so different seeing the people crossing at Check Point Charlie  we were retired living in New Mexico when the wall came down. A friends daughter was teaching for DOD school  in the west and sent her parents pieces of the wall.
I was so happy for the German families reunification.

comments.author: @otisblack3921
comments.text: My maternal grandparents were East German.   I remember visiting and meeting them for the one and only time in 1979 when I was 16 years old and the country was still under communist rule.   We would have to ride a bike every morning to the bakery by 6 am if you had any hope in making a purchase before stock ran out.   There was no refrigerator in the house. Just a cool pantry.   My grandparents to us to the fanciest restaraunt in East Berlin.   We tried to order beef.   We tried to order chicken.   We tried to order veal.   Each request was met with a “we don’t have that today”.    You could either get pork or mutton.   At the best restaraunt in the country.   It was obvious that anything of value was taken out the country at the end of WWII.    While the allies sunk billions into rebuilding the west, the east was left in rubble.  Yet the people were magnificent.   Not proud, not patriotic, yet not resentful nor prone to a victim mentality.   They laughed the same way we did.   They celebrated victories and mourned losses like all of us do.   One can argue that they can’t miss what they’ve never known and there is truth in that.   But it is within the human spirit to strive for improvement and to look for purpose.  This is where socialism and its bedfellow propaganda are at their most insidious.   Too young to really grasp the ideal at the time….and too entitled to even comprehend my own vulnerability.   You never know what you don’t know, right?  Still a life changing experience even as I continue  failing at giving it proper context
